*For engineers deciding whether to put a gateway between an application and several LLM deployments. No Azure API Management experience is assumed.*

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
### The short answer

A gateway cannot create quota. In every test, quota set the ceiling on how much work got done. What the gateway could change was which region absorbed a shortfall, and that mattered in only one of the situations I tested.

- **Every region out of quota at once:** the gateway made no useful difference. Spreading load, retrying inside the gateway and tuning weights nearly all landed in the same 16-18% band for a 200-request burst. With an even split, a circuit breaker (a rule that stops sending to a region after repeated failures) cut that to 4.5%. Only a client that sleeps until the service says to retry got nearly everything through (99.5%), at about 30 seconds a call.
- **Only the primary region out of quota (the one taking most of the traffic), two with room:** this is where a gateway helps, if it is set up for it. Retrying inside the gateway did nothing on its own (68-69%, against 70% with no recovery). Retries plus a circuit breaker that counts quota errors raised success to 96.5%, or 99.3% when the breaker tripped on the first failure (one run). A client that simply tried the primary region and then the next reached 100%, although that comparison is not like for like (see the limits at the end).
- **Five minutes of steady load:** the four setups I tried all finished within about 6% of what the quota allowed.

So the case for APIM here is about operations, not throughput: one endpoint for callers, credentials kept in one place, and central policy and monitoring. Once the breaker is set up, performance was close to a failover chain written into the client.
:::

## The problem

Large language model (LLM) deployments are rationed. Each Azure AI Foundry deployment has a quota in tokens per minute (TPM). When it is used up, the service does not slow down. It refuses the call with HTTP 429 ("Too Many Requests") and says when to try again.

A common answer is to deploy the same model in several regions and fall back between them. The simplest version lives in the client: try the first region, then the next, then the last, moving on only after a 429. That is a sensible safety net for one request. It is a poor way to share quota if every region is short at once, because the spare regions have nothing to spare.

The question is what a gateway adds. Azure API Management (APIM) can sit between callers and the regions and apply rules to every call. I put one in front of three Foundry deployments, set the quotas low enough to exhaust them on demand, and changed one setting at a time. The aim is to understand which gateway settings help when quota runs out, in which situation, and which only look helpful.

## Just enough APIM

Eight ideas are enough to follow every experiment.

| Term | What it means here |
|---|---|
| **Gateway** | APIM, a proxy that every caller talks to. It applies *policies* (rules) to each request as it passes through. |
| **Policy sections** | Policies run in order: *inbound* (before the backend is called), *backend* (the call itself), *outbound* (the response). Retry lives in the backend section. |
| **Backend pool** | A [group of endpoints behind one name](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/api-management/backends). Here, the three Foundry regions. The gateway picks one for each call. |
| **Weights** | The share of traffic each pool member gets. **90/5/5** means 90% to UK South and 5% each to West Europe and Sweden Central. **Even** means 33/33/34. |
| **429, 5xx and 503** | A 429 means "out of quota, try later", usually with a `Retry-After` header saying when. A 5xx means the backend itself is failing. When the gateway's own retries all fail, it answers with a 503, so a caller that only watches for 429 never sees the quota error. |
| **Circuit breaker** | After a set number of failures, a backend is taken out of the pool for a while (60 seconds here). This is called tripping. You choose which status codes count as failures: 429 and 5xx, or 5xx only. |
| **Client retry and pool retry** | Client retry: the caller sends the call again. [Pool retry](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/api-management/retry-policy): the gateway sends it again to the pool, before the caller sees a failure. |
| **Quota ceiling** | Quota is counted in one-minute windows (a *quota minute*). In each window a region completed only so many requests and refused the rest with a 429 until the next window. I measured that ceiling (see below), because it turned out to explain most of the results. |

Two kinds of comparison run through the article. Most results are set against a **control**, a run with an even split and no policies. Some runs skip the gateway and call Foundry **directly** from the client. Three names for test shape also recur. A **burst** is a short run of 200 requests fired as fast as 20 simulated callers can send them. A **sustained** run is five minutes of continuous load, which crosses several quota minutes. A **constant-rate** run sends a fixed number of requests every second for five minutes, whether or not earlier ones have been answered.

### The levers

Four settings changed between runs. Client retry and pool retry are two positions of the same lever: the caller tries again, the gateway tries the pool again, or both with the caller as a backstop.

| Lever | What it changes | Effect on success rate | Effect on throughput |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Pool weights** | How often each region is chosen | Changes who runs out first, not the total quota. In bursts it did not change how many calls completed | None that I could separate from noise |
| **Circuit breaker** | Drops a backend for 60 seconds after N failures | Helps when other regions have room and something retries onto them. With every region short, it empties the pool and **cuts** success | Calls refused within milliseconds; about 5% fewer completions over five minutes |
| **Gateway request cap** | Rejects calls at the gateway, before Foundry, once a subscriber exceeds N calls a minute ([`rate-limit-by-key`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/api-management/rate-limit-by-key-policy)) | A tight cap refuses work that would have succeeded | Instant refusals look busy and deliver nothing |
| **Retry** | Where the second attempt happens: client or pool | Sleeping for `Retry-After` eventually succeeds. Pool retry succeeds only if a healthy region exists and the pool steers there | Client sleeps wreck throughput; pool retry cost nothing over five minutes |

## Measuring the outcome

Four numbers describe each run.

| Metric | Definition | The question it answers |
|---|---|---|
| **Completions** | Requests that eventually got a valid answer | How much work was actually done? |
| **Success rate** | Completions ÷ original requests | Did the caller get an answer? |
| **Throughput** | Original requests ÷ elapsed seconds | How quickly are requests being dealt with? |
| **Goodput** | Completions ÷ elapsed seconds (throughput × success rate) | How much useful work landed per second? |

"Eventual" and "original" matter because of retries. A call that fails, is retried and then succeeds counts once, as a success. Retries are not counted as extra requests, so a retry storm cannot make a run look faster.

A worked example: 100 requests, 90 of them end in a 200 (some after retries), and the whole test takes 10 seconds. Success rate is 90%, throughput is 10 a second, and goodput is 9 a second.

Goodput matters because each of the other two can be gamed. A gateway that refuses every call instantly has excellent throughput and no goodput. A client that sleeps for 30 seconds per call has near-perfect success rate and almost no throughput. Goodput is low for both.

Goodput has limits, so two cautions apply throughout. In a burst the number of completions is capped by the quota, so goodput mostly reflects how quickly the run ended: a run of fast refusals can look good on goodput while completing no more than a slow one. And comparisons are only fair within a group of runs that share a quota and a load shape. Cards in the tabs below say which group they belong to.

## How the tests ran

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Gateway | APIM Developer tier, UK South |
| Backends | 3 × Azure AI Foundry: UK South, West Europe, Sweden Central |
| Model | `gpt-4.1-mini`, `max_tokens: 5`, one fixed prompt |
| Quota | 10,000 TPM per region for the first runs, low enough that regions are exhausted in seconds. 60,000 TPM per region for the later runs |
| Load generator | [Grafana k6](https://k6.io) on my laptop |
| Burst run | 200 requests (300 for one run), 20 virtual users (concurrent simulated callers) |
| Sustained run | 5 minutes, 20 virtual users, each sending its next request as soon as the last returns |
| Constant-rate run | 2 requests a second for 5 minutes (1 a second for the calibration run) |
| Between runs | A 60-second wait, so a tripped breaker from the previous run has reset |
| Success | An HTTP 200. The 60,000 TPM runs and the constant-rate runs also required a valid response body. The 200s in the earlier bursts took about 280 to 550 ms, which is what real completions look like |

The low quota exists so that one region can be exhausted in a burst instead of after an hour of polite traffic. The shape of the problem is what I care about: one region, or all of them, run out, and the gateway either notices or does not. One caution about the word "quota": the ceiling I measured is well below Azure's documented ratio (see below), and I have not confirmed in the portal which limit produced the 429s. Read "quota" in this article as "the limit these deployments enforced". The Terraform, the k6 scripts and the results are in
<a href="https://github.com/r-leyshon/azure-load-balance-perf" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">r-leyshon/azure-load-balance-perf</a>.

Two choices need explaining. First, **why a constant rate?** With 20 callers that each send again as soon as they get an answer, a setup that refuses quickly sees far more requests per second than one that responds slowly, so the setups are not facing the same load. A constant-rate run removes that: requests arrive at a fixed pace whatever the gateway does. Second, **the calibration run.** Before trusting any constant-rate result I ran an even split at half the rate with nothing wrong, which should succeed almost completely. If it does not, the rate is beyond what the regions can serve and every setup will converge on the same ceiling. It succeeded 100%.

### Tier and auth, as context

The pool, breaker, pool retry and managed identity used here are available on every [API Management tier](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/api-management/api-management-features) except Consumption, which has no backend circuit breaker. I used Developer: it has the features, no SLA, and one gateway unit. Callers present a subscription key to the gateway, and the gateway calls Foundry with a managed identity (an Azure-issued identity, so no model keys sit on the gateway). Neither was varied between runs.
:::

## What the experiments show

Every run is listed in [All the runs](#all-the-runs) at the end. This section is the argument they support, in three situations that differ in how much quota was left.

| Situation | What helped | What did not | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Every region out of quota | A client that waits for `Retry-After`: 99.5%, at about 30 s a call | Weights, retries and most breaker settings all landed on the same 16.5-18.5%. A breaker on 429 with an even split fell to 4.5% | 28 bursts at 10,000 TPM |
| Only the primary region out of quota | Pool retry with a breaker on 429: 96.5%, or 99.3% tripping on the first failure. A client that tries the next region: 100% | Pool retry alone: 68.5%. A breaker on 5xx only: 69.9% | 16 constant-rate runs at 60,000 TPM |
| Quota to spare, steady load | Nothing needed: the control did as well as anything (1,079 of a 1,080 ceiling) | The breaker cost about 5% of completions | 4 five-minute runs, 3 bursts |

### One idea explains most of the numbers

Each region behaved as if it completed a fixed number of requests a quota minute and refused the rest. I measured that ceiling at about 12 requests a minute per region at 10,000 TPM, and about 72 at 60,000 TPM, six times more for six times the quota. Azure's usual ratio is about 6 requests a minute for every 1,000 TPM of quota, which would be about 60 a minute at 10,000 TPM. I measured about 12, and I did not confirm the configured limits in the portal, so read the figures as measured, not as a rule.

Four results line up with those figures. They are consistency checks, not advance predictions: I did not set the ceiling from one result and test it on the others.

- Across three regions at 10,000 TPM, the ceiling is 36 requests a minute. The 200-request bursts finished in a few seconds and completed 33 to 37.
- At 60,000 TPM it is 216 a minute, which is more than a 200-request burst needs. Those bursts completed 90-96%.
- Over five minutes at 60,000 TPM, the ceiling is 1,080 completions. Four different setups completed between 1,021 and 1,079.
- With 90% of traffic aimed at one region at 60,000 TPM, that region is offered about 108 requests a minute against a ceiling near 72. UK South can therefore serve about two thirds of what it is sent, and the other 10% of calls go to idle regions that serve everything. Expected success is 0.9 × 72/108 + 0.1 = 70%, which is what a run with no recovery delivered.

A gateway moves requests between regions. It cannot raise the ceiling. What it can do is decide who absorbs the shortfall.

### 1. Every region out of quota (10,000 TPM bursts)

**A gateway on its own adds nothing.** The control (even split, no policies) completed 17.5% of requests, 35 of 200. Calling Foundry directly with an even split gave the same 17.5%. The gateway is a place to put policies. It is not a source of quota.

**Walking the regions in order does not help either.** The client-side safety net described in [The problem](#the-problem) completed 16.5% and made 567 HTTP calls to land 33 successes. When every region is short, a fallback order moves demand around and creates no tokens.

**Most settings land on the same result.** Seventeen of the 28 runs completed between 33 and 37 requests (16.5-18.5%), which I call the plateau. They include the control, calling the regions directly, skewed and unskewed weights, a breaker that only counts 5xx, tripping on the first failure instead of the third, and pool retry with or without a breaker. My reading is that a burst that finishes in seconds can only draw on about one minute of quota, so the setups that kept answering at that pace all hit the same wall.

**Policies can make things worse.** A circuit breaker that counts 429s, on an even split, cut a burst to 4.5% in both runs. It removes exhausted regions one by one, and then callers have nowhere to go. With skewed weights the same kind of breaker usually stayed on the plateau (six of seven runs) and once fell to 5.5%, so whether it collapses depends on timing within the quota minute. A gateway cap below real demand refuses calls that would have succeeded (3.5%). Combine weights, a breaker and a cap and you get the busiest run (238 requests a second) with no completions at all. The gateway was fast at saying no. This is what goodput is for.

**With client retry, either wait out the whole quota minute or do not bother.** Immediate retry matched the control. Fixed-pause and backoff retries completed slightly fewer (12-13%), which is within the run-to-run swing described below, so I read them as no better. A pause shorter than the quota minute cannot help, because the retry arrives in the same exhausted window. Sleeping for the `Retry-After` value reached 99.5%, but the median time to success was about 30 seconds and goodput 0.44 a second. That is fine for a nightly job and wrong for a chat request. It also completes more only because it runs for longer: 199 completions took 456 seconds, which spans several quota minutes.

**Stacked retries add little.** A breaker plus a client `Retry-After`, with no pool retry, completed 72 of 200 (36%) in 124 seconds, which is two minutes' worth at 36 a minute. With pool retry added, the run ended in 2.5 seconds, so the client's 30-second sleep never fired and the result was the plateau again.

**Identical configurations gave different answers.** Pool retry with a breaker on 429 and 5xx at 90/5/5 completed 18.0% on one run and 5.5% on its repeat. Where in the quota minute a burst lands matters at this scale, so read any single burst result as a range, 5-18% here, not a point.

The chart below shows every 200-request burst. **X** is success rate. **Y** is throughput: original requests per second, on a log scale because the runs span more than two orders of magnitude. Retries inflate the raw call rate, so I count original requests only, and a flood of retries should not look like a win. The grey curves are lines of constant goodput, because goodput is throughput × success rate. The diamonds are the 60,000 TPM runs. Hover a point for its name, run id and numbers. Sustained and constant-rate runs are not on the chart, because goodput is not comparable between runs of different quota and load shape.

```{=html}
<iframe
  class="shaded_box"
  title="Interactive scatter of the APIM burst experiments"
  src="/./www/24-apim-load-balance-perf/scatter.html"
  loading="lazy"
  referrerpolicy="no-referrer"
  style="display:block;width:100%;max-width:960px;height:720px;margin:0 auto;border:none;overflow:hidden;">
</iframe>
<p class="rp-fig" style="text-align:center;margin-top:.35rem;color:#52606d;">goodput = throughput × success rate</p>
```

Top-right is where an interactive API wants to be: high success and high throughput. Bottom-left is "most calls fail". Hard against the right edge and low down is "they succeed, eventually, if the user is prepared to wait half a minute". The cluster in the left half is the plateau, which is the main message of the chart: most 10,000 TPM runs end up in the same place whatever was configured.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
### High success is not the same as a good result

Waiting for `Retry-After` gets almost every call a 200 at about half a request a second. The run with the 500-a-minute cap is the mirror image: the gateway was quick and nobody got a completion. Success rate says whether the work was done, goodput says how quickly. When a product needs both, read both.
:::

### 2. Quota to spare (60,000 TPM bursts)

With six times the quota, 200 requests fit within one minute's allowance, and pool retry with no breaker completed 193 (96.5%), 190 (95.0%) and 181 (90.5%) in three runs. Skewing the weights to 90/5/5 made no visible difference (95.0%). The shortfall of 4-10% is small, and I did not investigate it. Uneven shares between regions are a plausible cause. These were single runs, and the two runs with the same configuration differ by six points.

This group is consistent with quota, not the gateway configuration, driving the plateau in section 1. It is not a controlled comparison, though: the two sets of bursts were run on different days, so other conditions may differ as well as the quota.

### 3. Five minutes of load (60,000 TPM)

Four setups ran for five minutes at 60,000 TPM, against a ceiling of 1,080 completions.

| Run | Completions | Of ceiling | Goodput | Success rate |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Control: even split, no policies | 1,079 | 99.9% | 3.59 /s | 4.6% |
| Pool retry, even split, no breaker | 1,078 | 99.8% | 3.58 /s | 20.5% |
| Breaker only, even split | 1,030 | 95.4% | 3.43 /s | 2.2% |
| Pool retry and breaker, 90/5/5 | 1,021 | 94.5% | 3.40 /s | 2.3% |

**Retry and routing did not change the amount of work done.** Pool retry cost nothing. Throwing three attempts at the pool did not drag the ceiling down.

**The setups with a breaker finished about 5% lower.** Both breaker setups sat just below the ceiling and both without one sat on it. Each setup ran once, though, and the pairs also differ in weights. A plausible reason is that a tripped region stays out for 60 seconds even though its quota refills sooner. Treat it as a small, tentative cost.

**Success rate misleads here.** Similar completions came out as about 2% for the breaker setups and 20.5% for pool retry (last column in the table). A setup that refuses calls quickly gets to send far more of them in the same five minutes, about 45,000 against 5,000. For sustained comparisons, count completions.

### 4. Only the primary region short (60,000 TPM, constant rate)

This is the situation where the gateway's configuration mattered. I sent 90% of the traffic to UK South at 2 requests a second. That deliberately overloads UK South, the primary region, and leaves West Europe and Sweden Central nearly idle. It resembles a deployment where one region has reserved (provisioned) capacity and the others are pay-as-you-go overflow. Each setup ran three times unless noted.

| Setup | Runs | Success (mean) | Range |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Direct, UK South first, then the next region | 3 | 100.0% | 100.0% |
| Pool retry, breaker on 429, trips on first failure | 1 | 99.3% | |
| Pool retry, breaker on 429 and 5xx | 3 | 96.5% | 93.5-98.0% |
| No recovery | 3 | 69.9% | 69.6-70.4% |
| Breaker on 5xx only | 1 | 69.9% | |
| Pool retry, no breaker | 3 | 68.5% | 68.2-69.1% |
| Pool retry, breaker on 5xx only | 1 | 68.2% | |

**With no recovery, success was 69.9%** (69.6-70.4). The result was very stable and matches the arithmetic above.

**Retry on its own did not help.** Retrying inside the gateway scored 68.5% (68.2-69.1), slightly below doing nothing in all three runs. I did not measure where the retries went. If each retry were a fresh weighted draw from the pool, some would land on a spare region and I would expect an improvement. The lack of one suggests most went back to the saturated region, but that is a guess.

**A breaker that ignores quota errors did nothing.** Counting only 5xx errors, it scored 69.9% on its own and 68.2% with retry (one run each). It never fires, because quota errors are 429s, not server errors.

**A breaker that counts 429s worked: 96.5%** (93.5-98.0). UK South returns 429s, the breaker takes it out of the pool for 60 seconds, and every retry can then only reach the two regions that have room. The shortfall from 100% is consistent with a few requests failing each minute before the breaker trips again, though I did not count failures per minute. Tripping on the first failure instead of the third scored 99.3% (one run, 4 of 600 failed), plausibly because fewer requests are lost before the breaker acts.

**Calling the regions directly from the client, UK South first and then the next, scored 100%** in all three runs. On average it made 0.40 to 0.50 extra calls per request, because the first try at UK South is refused (I counted calls in two of the three runs). The median time to a successful answer was 363-402 ms, against 333-352 ms for the gateway setups that worked, so roughly 25-65 ms slower, which is the cost of the wasted first call. Treat the 100% with care. The client always tried UK South first, while the gateway used a 90/5/5 weighted pool, so the two were not given the same job.

The lever that failed in section 1, a breaker that counts 429s, is the one that makes the gateway work here. When every region is short, the breaker empties the pool. When only the primary is short, it steers retries to the regions that have room. The only difference is whether there was spare quota somewhere else.

### What did not matter

In bursts, none of these changed the result: weights (even, 60/25/15, 70/15/15, 80/10/10 and 90/5/5 all sat at 16-18% when quota was short), the breaker's trip count, a breaker that counts only 5xx, and pool retry. Over five minutes, retry and routing did not change completions either.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
### A note on noise: how many times each result was seen

Most 10,000 TPM burst runs were single runs of one to two seconds. The one configuration that was repeated gave 18.0% and 5.5%, so a swing of that size can happen with nothing changed, and differences of a few points between bursts are ties. Only effects that repeat, or are far larger, are worth reading: the breaker on an even split gave 4.5% twice, and sleeping for `Retry-After` gave about 99% twice. The 60,000 TPM bursts and the five-minute runs are single runs. The constant-rate setups ran three times, except the 5xx-only breaker setups and the one-failure trip run, which were single runs. Those repeats were tight for the setups that failed (69.6-70.4%, 68.2-69.1%) and wide for the one that worked (93.5-98.0%).
:::

## What this means for your design

These are consequences of what I measured, not a checklist.

- **Find out which situation you are in first.** If every region is short, no gateway setting will help much, and the options are more quota, a smaller workload, or callers that can wait. If one region is short and others have room, the gateway can reallocate.
- **Buy quota before tuning routing.** When every region was short, quota moved the result by more than any setting did, and sustained throughput was the same whichever setting I used.
- **A breaker that counts 429s is a bet that another region has room.** It made the one-region-short case work (70% to 96.5%) and it emptied the pool in even-split bursts when every region was short (4.5% both times). With a low trip count it closed most of the remaining gap (99.3%, one run). That is a thing to test against your own failure modes, not a rule: I did not test it when fallbacks were near their own limit, or with one-off errors, where a single failure would remove a region for 60 seconds.
- **Retry alone does not redirect traffic.** In the one-region-short case, retrying inside the gateway did nothing without a breaker to remove the saturated region. Do not assume a retry will find a different region.
- **A breaker that counts only 5xx is safe and, under quota errors, invisible.** It protects against broken backends. It will not help with quota.
- **Client `Retry-After` is a batch tool.** It is the right behaviour when work can wait for the quota minute. It must also handle a 503, because when the gateway's own retries fail the caller sees a 503, not a 429.
- **A client-side failover chain is a real alternative.** It reached 100% when one region was short, at the cost of credentials for every region, extra calls, and no central policy or visibility. APIM's case here is operational. Whether that is worth a point or two of success is your decision, and I did not test a chain against the gateway under the same weights.
- **A gateway request cap protects against load you meant to refuse.** Set below the traffic you intend to serve, it refuses everything you wanted to serve.

## Where this stops applying

- **Sustained load was tested at 60,000 TPM only.** The burst results at 10,000 TPM do not tell you how a small quota behaves over time.
- **Short tests and small quota.** The burst runs finish in seconds and quota minutes are short. Treat the ratios and failure modes as the finding, not absolute request rates.
- **Single runs.** The 60,000 TPM bursts, the sustained runs, the one-failure trip run and the 5xx-only breaker setups ran once, as described in the note on noise.
- **A direct client versus APIM is not like for like.** The client sends every call to UK South first, the gateway used a 90/5/5 weighted pool. I did not count calls per region.
- **Why retry alone did not help is unknown.** I measured the outcome, not where each retry went.
- **Priority groups were not tested.** Every region in my pool had the same priority and traffic was steered by weight. APIM can also rank backends so that fallback regions are used only when the primary is unavailable, which is a natural fit for one primary and several fallbacks. A client-side chain beating my gateway setup says nothing about that configuration.
- **The limit behind the 429s is unconfirmed.** The measured ceiling is about five times below Azure's usual ratio, and I have not checked which limit the 429 responses named.
- **One gateway unit, no SLA.** A higher tier would not raise goodput in this study, because the quota on each region was the ceiling. On multi-unit tiers, breaker state is per instance and, as Microsoft notes in the [backends documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/api-management/backends), pool load balancing is approximate because instances do not share that state. One unit's trip is not everyone's trip.
- **Success means a valid answer.** I did not judge answer quality, only that a response came back.
- **Laptop load.** k6 ran from my machine, so absolute latency includes that round trip. Comparisons between runs share the path.
- **Alternatives I did not test.** APIM also documents an [LLM token-limit policy](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/api-management/llm-token-limit-policy), which limits tokens rather than requests. My gateway cap counted requests per minute.

```{=html}
<script>
(function () {
  var reduce = window.matchMedia("(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)").matches;
  function parseValue(text) {
    var match = String(text).trim().match(/^([\d.]+)(.*)$/);
    if (!match) return null;
    return { n: parseFloat(match[1]), suffix: match[2] || "", d: (match[1].split(".")[1] || "").length };
  }
  document.querySelectorAll(".exp-grid .exp-card").forEach(function (card) {
    var bars = [];
    card.querySelectorAll(".mbar").forEach(function (row) {
      var fill = row.querySelector(".track i");
      var label = row.querySelector(".v");
      if (!fill || !label) return;
      var pct = parseFloat(getComputedStyle(fill).getPropertyValue("--pct")) || parseFloat(fill.style.getPropertyValue("--pct")) || 0;
      var parsed = parseValue(label.textContent);
      if (!parsed) return;
      bars.push({ fill: fill, label: label, pct: pct, n: parsed.n, suffix: parsed.suffix, d: parsed.d });
      if (!reduce) {
        fill.style.setProperty("--pct", "0");
        label.textContent = (0).toFixed(parsed.d) + parsed.suffix;
      }
    });
    if (!bars.length || reduce || !("IntersectionObserver" in window)) return;
    var played = false;
    var observer = new IntersectionObserver(function (entries) {
      if (played || !entries.some(function (e) { return e.isIntersecting; })) return;
      played = true;
      observer.disconnect();
      var start = performance.now();
      var duration = 900;
      function frame(now) {
        var t = Math.min(1, (now - start) / duration);
        var eased = 1 - Math.pow(1 - t, 3);
        bars.forEach(function (bar) {
          bar.fill.style.setProperty("--pct", String(bar.pct * eased));
          bar.label.textContent = (bar.n * eased).toFixed(bar.d) + bar.suffix;
        });
        if (t < 1) requestAnimationFrame(frame);
      }
      requestAnimationFrame(frame);
    }, { threshold: 0.35 });
    observer.observe(card);
  });
})();
</script>
```
